title: Monsoon Health Myths Indian Doctors Want You to Stop Believing
excerpt: From the idea that antibiotics fix every fever to the misconception that mosquitoes only breed in dirty water, doctors are debunking dangerous monsoon myths as seasonal infections spike across India.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Seasonal infection tests more than doubled from July to September 2025, with over 2,100 tests in early 2026.
  • Dengue-carrying Aedes mosquitoes bite during the day and breed in clean stagnant water, not just dirty drains.
  • Self-medicating with antibiotics for viral fevers increases drug resistance without aiding recovery.
  • Kerala reported 186 deaths from communicable diseases in 2026, prompting health advisories across states.

Every monsoon season, a familiar cycle begins: temperatures drop, the rains arrive, and WhatsApp groups light up with health advice ranging from sensible to dangerously wrong. Doctors across India are pushing back against persistent myths they say delay treatment, fuel antibiotic resistance, and leave people vulnerable to infections that are entirely preventable.

The stakes are real. Communicable diseases have claimed 186 lives in Kerala this year, with 48 deaths reported in the first 20 days of June alone, according to state health data. Cases of dengue, Shigella, influenza, and leptospirosis are climbing nationwide as the 2026 monsoon brings erratic rainfall and high humidity.

The Antibiotics Myth

The most dangerous misconception, doctors say, is the reflexive reach for antibiotics at the first sign of fever.

"Many patients seek medical care only after trying home remedies or over-the-counter medicines for several days. By then, the underlying infection may have already progressed, increasing the risk of serious complications."

— Dr. Rajesh Kumar, Director of Internal Medicine, Paras Health Gurugram

Antibiotics target bacteria, not viruses — and most monsoon fevers, from influenza to chikungunya, are viral. Taking antibiotics for a viral infection does nothing to speed recovery but does contribute to drug resistance, a growing crisis in India. Indian Council of Medical Research data show that E. coli susceptibility to the antibiotic imipenem fell from 86% in 2016 to 64% in 2021, with more than half of isolates in some regions now classified as multidrug-resistant.

Dr. Shelly Mahajan, Lab Director at Mahajan Imaging & Labs, said the real problem is that many monsoon infections present nearly identical symptoms in their early stages. "A fever may be caused by a viral infection, dengue, malaria, typhoid or hepatitis, but each requires a different clinical approach," she said. "Relying on symptoms alone or starting medication without proper evaluation can delay diagnosis and increase the risk of complications."

Mosquitoes Don't Wait for Nightfall — or Dirty Water

Two of the most stubborn myths involve mosquito behaviour. Many people believe mosquitoes bite only at night and breed exclusively in dirty water. Both are wrong.

The Aedes mosquito, which transmits dengue and chikungunya, is a daytime biter. And it breeds preferentially in clean, stagnant water — the kind that collects in flower pots, air-cooler trays, and uncovered water tanks, not open sewage drains.

Dr. Niraj Kumar, Senior Consultant in Internal Medicine at ShardaCare Healthcity, pointed to this misconception directly: "Correcting common misconceptions, such as mosquitoes breeding only in dirty water or every fever requiring antibiotics, can significantly reduce the burden of seasonal infections."

What the Testing Data Shows

Diagnostic trends at Mahajan Imaging & Labs illustrate the seasonal surge. The lab conducted roughly 400–490 tests per month for seasonal infectious diseases from May to July 2025, before volumes jumped to 937 in August and peaked at 1,128 in September. Even after the monsoon's peak, testing remained elevated at 597 in October. In the first six months of 2026, the lab has already performed 2,107 tests for dengue, malaria, chikungunya, hepatitis A, leptospirosis, and typhoid.

Health authorities across multiple states have issued public advisories. Telangana's health department is urging citizens to wash hands regularly and avoid stale food. Meghalaya's advisory recommends mosquito nets, full-sleeved clothing, and avoiding contact with floodwater.

Other Myths That Persist

Doctors are also challenging smaller but widespread beliefs: that you need less water during the monsoon because you feel less thirsty (dehydration remains a risk, since the body continues losing fluids through sweat); that hot street food is safe (contamination from rainwater and poor hygiene makes it risky regardless of temperature); and that getting drenched in rain guarantees illness (viruses cause infection, not rain itself — though prolonged exposure can lower immune defenses).

Dr. Sneha Tirpude, a senior consultant pulmonologist, noted that respiratory illnesses are also rising during this monsoon. "The combination of high humidity, changing temperatures and increased exposure to allergens" is driving cases of asthma and seasonal respiratory infections, she said.

What Doctors Actually Recommend

The consensus is straightforward: persistent fever lasting more than two days, especially with severe weakness, vomiting, bleeding, or difficulty breathing, warrants immediate clinical evaluation — not a trip to the pharmacy. Drink filtered or boiled water. Eliminate stagnant water around homes. Apply mosquito repellent during the day, not just at night. And complete any prescribed antibiotic course fully rather than stopping when symptoms improve.

The monsoon is expected to intensify in the coming weeks. For the Indian diaspora visiting family or advising relatives from abroad, knowing which health tips to trust — and which to challenge — could matter more than usual this season.
